---
title: Lua filters
---

Quarto documents can be transformed with [Pandoc-style Lua
filters](https://pandoc.org/lua-filters.html). List filters in the
document (or project) metadata:

``` yaml
---
title: My document
filters:
  - my-filter.lua
---
```

## Element filters

A filter file defines functions named after the AST elements it wants to
transform. Each function receives the element and may return a
replacement (or `nil` to keep the element unchanged):

``` lua
function Str(el)
  return pandoc.Str(el.text:upper())
end

function Header(el)
  el.level = el.level + 1
  return el
end
```

## Whole-document handlers: `Meta` and `Pandoc`

Beyond element functions, a filter can define document-level handlers:

- `function Meta(meta)` receives the document metadata after the element
  traversal (so it can observe anything element functions computed).
  Return the (possibly modified) `meta`, or `nil` to leave metadata
  unchanged.
- `function Pandoc(doc)` receives the whole document (`doc.blocks`,
  `doc.meta`) last of all, and may return a replacement document.
  (`Doc` is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

``` lua
function Meta(meta)
  meta.subtitle = 'Rendered ' .. os.date('%Y-%m-%d')
  return meta
end

function Pandoc(doc)
  doc.blocks:insert(pandoc.HorizontalRule())
  return doc
end
```

With the default (typewise) traversal the order is: element functions,
then `Meta`, then `Pandoc`. Setting `traverse = 'topdown'` reverses it:
`Pandoc` first, then `Meta`, then a top-down element walk. Element
functions also traverse metadata values — a `Str` function will visit
the words of your `title` as well as your document body, exactly as in
Pandoc.

## Two ways to organize a filter

Everything above defines handlers as **global functions**. A filter may
instead **return a table** of them, which keeps the handlers out of the
global namespace:

``` lua
return {
  Str = function(el)
    return pandoc.Str(el.text:upper())
  end,
}
```

Both forms are equivalent, and both work in Pandoc. Set `traverse` as a
key of the table rather than as a global when you use this form:

``` lua
return {
  traverse = 'topdown',
  Div = function(el) ... end,
}
```

::: callout-important
## A returned table replaces the globals

If a script both defines global handlers and returns a table, **only the
returned table runs** — the globals are ignored entirely. This follows
Pandoc.

It also means an *empty* returned table silently disables every global
handler in the file, and that an accidental `return nil` at the end of a
script is an error rather than a no-op ([`Q-11-6`](../../errors/lua/Q-11-6.qmd)).
To use your global functions, end the script without returning anything
at all.
:::

## Several passes in a fixed order

Returning a *list* of handler tables runs each one as a separate pass
over the whole document, in order. Each pass sees the previous pass's
output:

``` lua
return {
  -- pass 1: mark the elements of interest
  { Div = function(el) ... end },
  -- pass 2: act on what pass 1 produced
  { Span = function(el) ... end },
}
```

Each entry carries its own `traverse` setting; a `traverse` on one entry
does not affect the others.

Reach for this when one transformation has to finish everywhere before
another begins. Within a single filter table you cannot get that
ordering by rearranging the handlers — the traversal order is fixed by
the document structure, not by the order you wrote them in. (A `Pandoc`
handler calling `doc:walk{...}` can also sequence passes by hand; a
returned list is the declarative way to say the same thing.)

## When a handler never runs

Handlers are dispatched **by name**, so a misspelled one is simply never
looked up. Quarto warns rather than leaving you to wonder
([`Q-11-7`](../../errors/lua/Q-11-7.qmd)):

```
Warning [Q-11-7]: Lua filter 'my-filter.lua' defines a handler 'Strs',
which is not an element type Quarto knows about, so it will never run.
Did you mean 'Str'?
```

If you keep helper functions on a returned filter table, they will be
warned about too. Make them `local` instead:

``` lua
local function shout(text)
  return text:upper()
end

return {
  Str = function(el) return pandoc.Str(shout(el.text)) end,
}
```

## How metadata looks from Lua

Metadata values appear as natural Lua values, following modern Pandoc's
conventions:

| metadata value | Lua value |
|----|----|
| string parsed as markdown (the default in front matter) | `Inlines` (or `Blocks`) |
| literal string (`!str`) | string |
| boolean | boolean |
| list | `pandoc.List` |
| mapping | table |

Quarto deliberately diverges from Pandoc in a few places, in favor of
its richer configuration model:

- **Numbers stay numbers.** `count: 3` reads as the Lua number `3`
  (Pandoc renders it as the string `'3'`). In return, a number or boolean
  is accepted wherever an Inline is expected and reads as `tostring`
  would print it: `pandoc.Strong(meta.count)` works, where Pandoc would
  reject `pandoc.Strong(3)`. Block positions stay strict.
- **Null reads as `nil`.** A key with an explicit YAML `~` looks absent
  from Lua; deleting a metadata key is `meta.key = nil`, and writing an
  explicit null is `quarto.config.null()`.
- Values Quarto tracks specially — `!path`, `!glob`, `!expr` tagged
  strings — appear as small typed values with a `.value` string
  property, and survive a filter round-trip losslessly.
- **Path-shaped keys are project-root-relative.** Keys Quarto knows hold
  file paths (`css`, `theme`, `include-in-header` and the other include
  slots, `bibliography`, `csl`, `reference-doc`, `template`, the `epub-*`
  files, a component's `src`) reach filters as `!path` values whose
  `.value` is the path relative to the project root (or absolute, for a
  file outside the project), whatever file declared it and whatever
  directory the current document is in. Quarto 1 handed filters the
  path relative to the input document instead, so a filter ported from
  Quarto 1 that opens such a file should build the absolute path with
  `quarto.project.directory` (see [Where the filter is running](#where-the-filter-is-running))
  rather than the document's directory.

Besides the `meta` argument of a `Meta` or `Pandoc` handler, every filter
can read the document metadata directly through `quarto.metadata.get("a.b")`
and the `meta` global, in the same shapes. The [lmd page](lmd.qmd#reaching-for-metadata)
describes both.

## Publishing extra files: `meta.resources` {#publishing-extra-files}

A document's `resources` list names files to copy into the output
directory with it. A filter can add to that list in two ways, and
both publish the file:

``` lua
function Meta(meta)
  quarto.doc.add_resource("data/extra.csv")  -- relative to the document

  local r = meta.resources or pandoc.List()  -- or edit the list itself
  r:insert("data/more.csv")
  meta.resources = r
  return meta
end
```

Removing an entry works only for entries Quarto added itself. Quarto
puts every local file that a markdown link points at into
`meta.resources`
([Linked files are copied](../projects/paths.qmd#linked-files-are-copied)),
and a filter can drop any of those. Entries the author declared under
`resources:` in YAML are always published, even if a filter removes
them, so a filter that rebuilds `meta` carelessly cannot unpublish
them.

Quarto adds the linked files *after* pre filters run, so only a
**post** filter (`at: post-quarto` or later) sees them and can remove
them:

``` {.yaml filename="page.qmd"}
filters:
  - at: post-quarto
    path: keep-big-files-out.lua
```

``` {.lua filename="keep-big-files-out.lua"}
function Meta(meta)
  local kept = pandoc.List()
  for _, r in ipairs(meta.resources or {}) do
    -- YAML entries arrive as Inlines, Quarto's as strings
    if not pandoc.utils.stringify(r):match("%.zip$") then
      kept:insert(r)
    end
  end
  meta.resources = kept
  return meta
end
```

A pre filter can instead turn link discovery off for the whole
document with `meta["resource-discovery"] = false`.

For Word, PowerPoint and Typst output, post filters run inside Pandoc,
after Quarto has already collected the document's resources, so they
cannot remove entries. Use `resource-discovery: false` (in YAML, or
from a pre filter) for those formats.

## Constructing configuration values: `quarto.config`

The `quarto.config` table mirrors Quarto's YAML tag system, so a filter
can create exactly the value a tag would have produced:

| Lua | YAML equivalent |
|----|----|
| `quarto.config.str('**text**')` | `key: !str "**text**"` (literal string) |
| `quarto.config.md('**text**')` | `key: !md "**text**"` (parsed markdown) |
| `quarto.config.path('style.css')` | `key: !path style.css` |
| `quarto.config.glob('posts/*.qmd')` | `key: !glob posts/*.qmd` |
| `quarto.config.expr('Sys.time()')` | `key: !expr Sys.time()` |
| `quarto.config.null()` | `key: ~` |

For example, to add a stylesheet path from a filter:

``` lua
function Meta(meta)
  meta.css = quarto.config.path('extra.css')
  return meta
end
```

## Equation numbers: the `quarto-eq-number` attribute

A labelled display equation (`$$…$$ {#eq-name}`) reaches your filters as a
`Span` whose `identifier` is the label and whose `attributes` carry the
equation's number under the reserved key `quarto-eq-number`. Quarto writes
the number into the page only after your filters have run, in the form the
selected math renderer understands (`\tag{N}` for MathJax and KaTeX, for
example). So a filter can change what is displayed by editing the
attribute, without touching the TeX:

``` lua
function Span(el)
  local n = el.attributes["quarto-eq-number"]
  if n then
    el.attributes["quarto-eq-number"] = "S" .. n   -- shows as (S1), (S2), …
    return el
  end
end
```

Delete the attribute (`el.attributes["quarto-eq-number"] = nil`) to leave
an equation unnumbered. The attribute exists only once cross-references
have been resolved, so list the filter *after* the `quarto` entry in
`filters:`; a filter listed before it runs too early to see the number.

## Parsing strings: `pandoc.read`

`pandoc.read(text, format)` parses a string into a document, so a filter or
an `{lmd}` cell can turn text into nodes. Three formats are available, and
`pandoc.readers` lists them:

- `"markdown"` (the default, also spelled `"qmd"`) reads Quarto Markdown,
  exactly as a document body is read.
- `"commonmark"` reads plain CommonMark.
- `"json"` reads a document in Pandoc's JSON format.

Quarto Markdown is strict on purpose: braces are reserved for attributes,
`$` starts math, a bare `[...]` is a span, and quotes must balance. That
suits text written as a document, and it is wrong for text that never was:
descriptions from a JSON schema, a database or a CMS. Such prose may contain
`{env:VAR}`, `$HOME` or `["a", "b"]`, which the `"markdown"` reader rejects
or rewrites. Read that kind of text with `"commonmark"`:

``` lua
local blocks = pandoc.read(entry.description, "commonmark").blocks
```

CommonMark has emphasis, links, code and lists, but no attributes, divs,
math or tables. Raw HTML in the text becomes raw `html` nodes, as in pandoc.

Format extensions (`"commonmark+smart"`) are accepted and ignored, for
every format.

Warnings about the text point into the string itself, labelled with the
line of the call, for example `doc.qmd[pandoc.read, line 14]`. This covers
the reader's own warnings and warnings a later step raises about the nodes
you returned.

## Tables, definition lists and figures built from Lua

Quarto's markdown has shorthand for three structures: a `::: {.list-table}`
div becomes a table, a `::: {.definition-list}` div becomes a definition list,
and a paragraph holding nothing but an image with alt text becomes a figure.
The reader rewrites those shapes as it parses, so by the time a filter runs,
the document holds `Table`, `DefinitionList` and `Figure` nodes, never the
shorthand.

The same rewrite is applied to markdown and JSON that `pandoc.read` returns,
and to what an `{lmd}` cell returns, so a cell that builds
`pandoc.Div({ rows }, pandoc.Attr("", {"list-table"}))` from nodes gets the
same `Table` the markdown would have. A list-table div with the wrong shape is
reported as `Q-2-35`, pointing at the cell that built it.

It is **not** applied to what a filter function returns. A filter that wants a
table returns a `pandoc.Table` (or the result of `pandoc.read`); a
`.list-table` div returned from a `Div` handler stays a div, as it does in
pandoc and in Quarto 1.

## Attaching scripts and stylesheets: `quarto.doc.add_html_dependency`

A filter that needs JavaScript or CSS in the rendered page registers an
**HTML dependency**. Quarto copies the files into the output and adds the
`<script>` and `<link>` tags for you:

``` lua
function Image(img)
  quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({
    name = 'zoom',
    version = '1.2.0',
    scripts = { 'zoom.js' },
    stylesheets = { 'zoom.css' },
  })
  return img
end
```

Paths are resolved relative to the filter's own directory, so an extension
can ship its assets alongside its `.lua` file and reference them by bare
name. An entry may also be written as a table with a `path` field —
`{ path = 'src/zoom.js' }` — which is equivalent to the bare string. The
copied file always keeps the base name of its path.

Dependencies are **deduplicated by name**, so it is safe — and intended — to
call `add_html_dependency` unconditionally from a handler that runs many
times. The example above fires once per image; only the first registration
does anything, and the rest are silently ignored.

Only `name` is required. Because the dependency only affects HTML output,
guard the call when your filter also targets other formats:

``` lua
if quarto.doc.is_format('html:js') then
  quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({ name = 'zoom', scripts = { 'zoom.js' } })
end
```

### Versions

The optional `version` keeps releases of the same dependency apart on disk.
Assets land under `site_libs/libs/{name}/`, with a version adding one level:

``` {.default}
_site/site_libs/libs/zoom/1.2.0/zoom.js   # with version = '1.2.0'
_site/site_libs/libs/zoom/zoom.js         # without
```

Declaring a version costs nothing and is worth doing for any dependency you
expect to update. Within a single document the first registration still
wins, so registering one name at two different versions reports a warning —
a page cannot sensibly load two copies of the same library.

### Fields not yet supported

Quarto 1 accepts several other fields on a dependency: `meta`, `links`,
`resources`, `serviceworkers`, and `head`. Quarto 2 does not implement them
yet, and warns once per dependency that names one, so a filter carried over
from Quarto 1 tells you what was dropped rather than failing. Any other
field is a typo and raises an error.

## Where the filter is running

A filter often needs to know which file it is processing and where the
project is, for example to build a link from the current page to a file at
the project root. Quarto 2 provides the same values Quarto 1 did:

``` lua
quarto.doc.input_file        -- absolute path of the file being rendered
quarto.doc.output_file       -- absolute path its output will be written to
quarto.project.directory     -- project root (nil outside a project)
quarto.project.output_directory  -- resolved output directory (nil outside a project)
quarto.project.offset        -- relative path from this file's directory back
                             -- to the project root: "." or "../..", forward
                             -- slashes (nil outside a project)
quarto.project.profile       -- pandoc.List of active profile names, possibly empty
```

So a page at `guides/intro.qmd` links to `appendix.qmd` at the root with:

``` lua
local href = quarto.project.offset .. "/appendix.html"
```

`PANDOC_STATE.input_files` (a one-element list holding `input_file`) and
`PANDOC_STATE.output_file` are set too, for filters written against pandoc's
API. The other `PANDOC_STATE` fields have no equivalent here and are `nil`.

### Environment variables and profiles

`os.getenv` sees the environment the render started with, plus the variables
your project's `_environment` files define (a real environment variable
always wins over a file). `QUARTO_PROFILE` is the active profile list, so a
filter sees `--profile drafts` the same way it sees
`QUARTO_PROFILE=drafts`:

``` lua
if os.getenv("QUARTO_PROFILE") == "drafts" then ... end
-- or, without string handling:
if quarto.project.profile:includes("drafts") then ... end
```

The environment is read once, before any filter runs, and every filter and
shortcode in the render sees the same values. The `{{< env NAME >}}`
shortcode reads the same snapshot, so it and a filter's `os.getenv` can
never disagree.

`pandoc.system.environment()` returns the same snapshot.

`pandoc.system.with_environment(env, callback)` replaces that environment for
the callback, as in Pandoc, but only for this filter. Documents can render in
parallel, so the real process environment never changes. Inside the callback:

- `os.getenv` and `pandoc.system.environment` see only the table you passed.
- Programs started with `pandoc.pipe` and `pandoc.system.command` get exactly
  that table as their environment, so include `PATH` if you need it.
- `io.popen` and `os.execute` raise an error, because their programs would get
  the real environment. This differs from Pandoc. Use `pandoc.pipe` or
  `pandoc.system.command` instead.
- `pandoc.system.xdg` still reads the real `XDG_*` variables.

### Working directory

`pandoc.system.with_working_directory(dir, callback)` changes the working
directory for the callback, but only for this filter. Documents can render in
parallel, so the real process directory never changes. Inside the callback:

- Relative paths passed to Quarto's Lua APIs, `pandoc.system`, `pandoc.path.exists`,
  `pandoc.mediabag`, `io.open`, `io.lines`, `io.input`, `io.output`, `os.remove`,
  `os.rename`, `loadfile` and `dofile` resolve against `dir`.
- Programs started with `pandoc.pipe` and `pandoc.system.command` start in `dir`.
- `io.popen` and `os.execute` raise an error, because their programs would start
  in the real directory. This differs from Pandoc. Use `pandoc.pipe` or
  `pandoc.system.command` instead.
- A relative entry in `package.path` still resolves against the real directory
  when `require` searches it. Modules beside your filter are not affected.

## Checking versions

`quarto.version` is the version of Quarto you are running, as a pandoc
`Version` object. It compares with strings and with other versions, prints
with `tostring`, and still works with `table.concat`:

``` lua
if quarto.version < "0.36" then
  quarto.log.warning("this filter needs Quarto 0.36 or newer")
end
print(tostring(quarto.version))           -- "0.36.0"
print(table.concat(quarto.version, "."))  -- "0.36.0"
quarto.version:must_be_at_least("0.36")   -- raises if older
```

`pandoc.types.Version` builds one from a string, a number or a list of
integers, and `PANDOC_VERSION` / `PANDOC_API_VERSION` are `Version` objects
as well. Quarto 2 releases are numbered `0.x` for now, so a filter that must
tell the two apart can test `quarto.version < "1"`: true here, false on
Quarto 1.

## Failing a render

Three ways to stop, from gentlest to bluntest:

- `quarto.error(message, element)` reports an error diagnostic pointing at
  the source location of `element`. The document fails; the rest of the
  project still renders.
- `error(message)` fails the document with a plain Lua error. The rest of
  the project still renders and the summary lists the failure.
- `os.exit(code)` also fails the document. Quarto 1 filters use it because
  there pandoc was a separate process; in Quarto 2 the filter runs inside
  the renderer, so `os.exit` is intercepted rather than ending the process.
  The failure message names the filter and the code; the remaining
  documents render, errors on them are still reported, and the render as a
  whole exits non-zero. `os.exit(0)` counts as a failure too, since no
  output was produced.

Prefer `quarto.error` in new code: it is the only one that points the author
at a location in their document.
